chunks: "You need a CSA when the shunt voltage can't be fed directly to the ADC. There are four typical reasons. One, the signal is too small.
A 10 milliohm shunt at 5 amps gives only 50 millivolts, while a 12-bit, 3. 3 volt ADC has a step of 0. 8 millivolts, so I'd resolve only about 80 milliamps per count.
A gain of 50 brings that to about 1. 6 milliamps and fills the ADC range. Two, common-mode.

If the shunt is on the high side of a 12, 24 or 48 volt bus, both ends are far above what the ADC or an ordinary op-amp can tolerate, and I need something that handles the common-mode and reports just the difference.
Three, level shifting and polarity. For bidirectional current I need the output biased around a reference, so the ADC can see both directions. Four, noise and accuracy.
Amplifying at the shunt, with a good differential input, keeps the signal well above the ADC's noise and rejects ground bounce.

I wouldn't need one if the ADC itself has a small differential input range or a programmable gain stage, for example a delta-sigma metering ADC with plus or minus 250 millivolts, or if I just want a rough overcurrent trip that a comparator can do directly, or if the current is so small I can use a large shunt."
